content: Whenever two people meet, there are really six people present: each as he sees himself, each as the other sees him, and each as he really is.
author: William James
sourceWork: Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking (1907)
story:
Rather than offering a polite platitude, this observation challenges how we navigate our inner lives. Holding onto anger is like clutching a glowing coal with the intent of throwing it at someone else—you are the one who gets burned. Retaliation only ties you tighter to the person who harmed you.

Across his life and work, William James saw how easily we surrender our tranquility to fear, vanity, and distraction. Forgiveness and composure are not signs of weakness or giving someone a pass. They are acts of fierce self-preservation, cutting the emotional chain that allows another person's bad behavior to ruin your peace of mind.
reflectionPrompt: How can acknowledging your vulnerability help you build deeper self-trust and inner peace?

practicalInsight: When someone triggers your temper today, take three slow breaths before responding. Do not give away your power for the sake of a quick comeback.
